plan.contextChunk: This figure has two panels, (a) and (b), each drawing a convex polygon over labeled points in the plane. In (a) a light gray polygon labeled Q_j fills the right portion; its boundary runs from p_0 at the bottom left up to p_j at the top, right through p_k and two unlabeled black dots, down the right side to p_2, and back along the bottom through p_1 to p_0. A darker gray triangle is attached along the left, with corners p_0, p_j, and a further point p_i lying outside to the left, so that the two shaded regions together form a larger polygon whose boundary now passes through p_i. In (b) the hull boundary is a thick gray chain from p_0 rightward to p_1, up the right side, and back across the top through p_j; at the left a thin-outlined light gray triangle has corners p_i, p_r just to its right, and p_0 at the bottom, and a point p_t sits inside that triangle. Dashed segments join p_i and p_r to p_t, and a small arc marks the angle at p_t. Placing the panels side by side contrasts a point that enlarges the hull with a point enclosed by three others and therefore incapable of being a hull vertex. The pair underpins the correctness argument for Graham's scan, where each newly considered point either joins the stack or forces an earlier point off it.

interactionPlan.concept: In Graham's scan, a non-left turn indicates that the previous point is enclosed by a triangle formed by the new point, the point before it, and the origin, meaning it cannot be part of the convex hull.
elements: Origin point p_0 at the bottom
Point p_1 at the bottom right
Several unlabeled black dots forming the right boundary curve
Point p_j at the top
Point p_k (only in panel a) on the boundary between the unlabeled points and p_j
Point p_i at the far left
Point p_r (only in panel b) on the boundary to the left of p_j
Point p_t (only in panel b) located inside the triangle p_0, p_r, p_i
Light gray convex polygon Q_j (only in panel a) filling the region from p_0 to p_j
Dark gray triangle (only in panel a) with vertices p_0, p_j, p_i
Light gray triangle (only in panel b) with vertices p_0, p_r, p_i and a thin dark outline
Thick gray hull boundary chain connecting p_0, p_1, ..., p_k, p_j, p_i (panel a) or p_0, p_1, ..., p_j, p_r, p_i (panel b)
Dashed segments (only in panel b) connecting p_r to p_t, and p_t to p_i
Angle arc (only in panel b) at p_t showing the reflex angle between p_r, p_t, and p_i
Labels for all named points (p_0, p_1, p_2, p_k, p_j, p_i, p_r, p_t) and the region Q_j

interactions.label: Scenario
interactions.teaches: Graham's scan handles two cases when considering a new point: it either forms a left turn and is added, or forms a non-left turn and forces the previous point to be removed.

interactions.label: Stack update step
interactions.teaches: Stepping through the stack update reveals that a non-left turn means the previous point lies inside a triangle formed by the new point, the point before it, and the origin—so it cannot be on the convex hull.
Selecting individual points highlights their specific role in the hull or the triangle that encloses them.

demo_steps.title: Adding a point
demo_steps.narration: When building the hull, Graham's scan sorts points by polar angle and considers them sequentially. Here, p_i is the next candidate.

demo_steps.title: Left turn expands hull
demo_steps.narration: If the new point p_i makes a left turn with the top of the stack p_j, it simply forms a new triangle with the origin, safely expanding the convex hull.

demo_steps.title: Detecting a non-left turn
demo_steps.narration: In a different scenario, if the next point p_i makes a right or straight turn from p_r through p_t, the algorithm detects a non-left turn.

demo_steps.title: Removing enclosed points
demo_steps.narration: Because of the non-left turn, p_t must lie inside the triangle formed by p_0, p_r, and p_i. It is enclosed and therefore popped from the hull stack.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because points are processed in polar angle order, a non-left turn implies the middle point lies inside the triangle formed by the other two and the origin, proving it cannot belong to the convex hull.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Show one panel at a time based on the toggle. Panel (a): Origin p_0 at bottom, points curving up to the right then left to p_j, forming a light gray convex polygon Q_j. A dark gray triangle connects p_0, p_j, and p_i (further left). Panel (b): Top points are p_r, p_t, p_i in increasing polar angle. p_t is pushed inwards so p_r -> p_t -> p_i forms a right turn. A thin-outlined light gray triangle spans p_0, p_r, p_i. p_t lies visibly inside this triangle, connected by dashed lines to p_r and p_i, with an angle arc at p_t. In both, trace the active hull boundary with a thick gray line (in panel b, it jumps from p_r directly to p_i).

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between the left-turn case in panel (a) and the nonleft-turn case in panel (b): the candidate point either expands the shaded hull or is shown inside the triangle, making clear how turn direction determines hull membership.
- Button for stepping through the Graham-scan stack update: each press tests the next labeled point, draws the relevant angle, and either pushes the point or removes the interior point, making clear why nonleft turns cannot remain on the convex hull.
- Click for p_i, p_j, p_r, or p_t: the selected point and its supporting triangle or hull edge highlight, making clear which surrounding points prove that it belongs on or inside the hull.

authoredContext: Theorem 33.1 (Correctness of Graham’s scan) If GRAHAM-SCAN executes on a set Q of points, where jQj _x0015_ 3, then at termination, the stack S consists of, from bottom to top, exactly the vertices of CH.Q/ in counterclockwise order. Proof After line 2, we have the sequence of points hp1; p2; : : : ; pmi. Let us define, for i D 2; 3; : : : ; m, the subset of points Qi D fp0; p1; : : : ; pi g. The points in Q Qm are those that were removed because they had the same polar angle relative to p0 as some point in Qm; these points are not in CH.Q/, and so CH.Qm/ D CH.Q/. Thus, it suffices to show that when GRAHAM-SCAN terminates, the stack S consists of the vertices of CH.Qm/ in counterclockwise order, when listed from bottom to top. Note that just as p0, p1, and pm are vertices of CH.Q/, the points p0, p1, and pi are all vertices of CH.Qi/. The proof uses the following loop invariant: At the start of each iteration of the for loop of lines 9–12, stack S consists of, from bottom to top, exactly the vertices of CH.Qi1/ in counterclockwise order

discrepancies: In scenario (a), the light gray polygon and the darker triangle lack thin stroke borders, causing the internal dividing line (p_0 to p_j) and the closing left edge (p_i to p_0) to be missing.
The angle arc at p_t in scenario (b) is drawn as a solid line, whereas the source figure uses a dotted/dashed line.
evaluation.notes: The generated interactive figure brilliantly translates the static textbook diagram into a step-by-step explainer for Graham's scan, with excellent label formatting and interaction logic, missing only a few minor styling details like the shape borders.
action_items: Add `.stroke({color: '#555', width: 1, linejoin: 'round'})` (or similar) to `polyA` and `triA` so the internal boundaries and closing edges are explicitly drawn in scenario (a).
Add `.stroke({..., dasharray: '4,4'})` to `angleArcB` so the angle indicator in scenario (b) appears dotted/dashed to match the source.
